# Aklilu Alemu
*Assistant Professor of Education Policy and Leadership at Madawalabu University, Bale Robe, Ethiopia *
#### ARTICLE INFO
*Keywords: * Determining factors Ethiopian universities Madawalabu university Research production
#### ABSTRACT
This study aimed to explore factors determining research production at Madda Walabu University. The study has employed a case study design to collect data through interviews, focus group discussions (FGDs), and document analysis. The study recruited six participants using purposive sampling techniques for interviews. Besides, seven discussants were selected using a purposeful sampling technique for FGD. The study revealed that the research practices at the three colleges were in their infancy stage. The primary factors that hindered research practice were lengthy research administrations, a lack of budget, a lack of facilities, and a lack of interest in conducting research. Hence, the study recommends that the university revisit research policies and provide authority and responsibility for schools to manage research in their respective schools. The study also recommended that the university should fulfill its facilities to achieve its vision.
### **1.** **Introduction **
Various scholars have published their findings on academics' research engagement and productivity. The focus of a vast number of empirical investigations on this subject has been on research engagement and productivity [(Banegas, 2018; Heng et al., 2020;](#page-6-0) [Henry et al., ](#page-6-0) [2020;](#page-6-0) [Nguyen et al., 2021](#page-7-0); Pinar & [Unlu, 2020)](#page-7-0). Many academics looking at this issue appear to have started with Borg'[s (2010)](#page-6-0) key work and used his definition of research involvement as a starting point. Some researchers have repeated Borg'[s (2010) ](#page-6-0)study in a new setting or changed his questionnaire to obtain data (Sadeghi & [Abutorabi, 2017](#page-7-0)).
[Borg (2010](#page-6-0), p. 391) defines research engagement as "engagement in research (i.e., by doing it) as well as engagement with research (i.e., by reading and using it)." This definition seems narrow in scope. Even if we base our definition on Borg's, the term "research engagement" encompasses various activities. Research engagement involves generating ideas and projects, conducting research, publishing, and publicizing research findings. This study defines research engagement beyond doing research and reading it.
Studies show a link between research and teaching in higher education institutions [(Gunawan, 2020](#page-6-0); [Iqbal et al., 2018;](#page-6-0) [Rawls, 2018](#page-7-0)). Continuous learning about the subject and teaching methods enhances effective teaching. Supporting this,[ Jenkins (2009)](#page-6-0) argues that empirical shreds of evidence should inform the teaching-learning process to enhance students' learning. Besides, faculties involved in research
practices are, in most cases, more useful in the teaching-learning process than those who do not participate [(Cocal et al., 2017](#page-6-0)). Various authors ([Brew et al., 2016;](#page-6-0)[ Nguyen, 2015](#page-7-0); Nguyen & [Klopper, 2014](#page-7-0)) recognize that universities run teaching and learning processes and research studies together.
The Ethiopian government enshrined national research endeavors in the Growth and Transformation Plans [(National Planning Commission, ](#page-7-0) [2016)](#page-7-0). According to the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia ([FDRE, ](#page-6-0) [2012)](#page-6-0), a Science, Technology, and Innovation Policy was implemented to tackle the community's critical social, economic, and technological problems. Similarly, the Ethiopian Education and Training Policy recommends that there should be a link between education and research in higher education, such as universities and technical and vocational education programs ([Transitional Government of Ethiopia (TGE), 1994](#page-7-0)). Within the Education and Training Policy framework, the Ethiopian Higher Education Proclamation (HEP) states in this way, "every institution shall undertake research that equips students with basic knowledge and skills that enable them to undertake further and relevant studies and research" ([FDRE, 2009](#page-6-0), p. 4990). Within the same proclamation, it underlines the production of research in this way: "Every institution shall ensure that all and every one of its academic staff engages in research focusing on developmental issues" [(FDRE, 2009](#page-6-0)). Two factors could incentivize Ethiopian university faculty to change their cultures to research-focused ones. On the one hand, as [FDRE (2009) ](#page-6-0) states, every faculty member should engage in the research process to

align with policy intentions. On the other hand, the existing deep-rooted African nations' problems encourage the faculty to be problem solvers.
Madda Walabu University, the target area of this study, is one of the country's second-generation universities, established in 2008. The university has re-engineered the Research and Community Service Directorate (RCSD) as one of its core business processes as of 2009. Accordingly, RCSD is the office that coordinates the university's research activities at the top level. Despite the establishment of the RCSD, no research has assessed the status of research undertaken at the university in particular or at second-generation universities in general. Thus, this study attempted to see the status of research practices at Madda Walabu University.
### *1.1.* *Statement of the problem *
Concerning research practices in Ethiopian higher education institutes (HEIs), different investigators have conducted research both at institutional (e.g., [Higher Education Relevance and Quality Agency ](#page-6-0) [(HERQA), 2008](#page-6-0)) and individual levels (e.g., [Amare, 2000](#page-6-0); [Derebssa, ](#page-6-0) [2004)](#page-6-0). Among institutional level research, the [HERQA (2008) ](#page-6-0)reports clearly show the problems related to research activities in different public HEIs in the country. The publication series focused on the institution's external quality and centered on relatively older universities (first-generation universities) in the country. HERQA incorporated a few government HEIs into the review and their reports, and the researcher presented them as follows: First, Hawassa University's reports clarify that although the university was engaged in research, it focused firmly on agricultural research. However, the main impediments to undertaking research were a shortage of academic staff, leaving no time for research, unattractive incentives, and financial problems, including low funding and poor financial management.
The report said the situation was even worse at Bahir Dar University. The university and the research publication office recognize that research is in its infancy throughout the university. According to the university's self-evaluation document, the number of staff involved in research in 2006–2007 was almost negligible (4%). The problem is similar at Mekelle University, whose legislation expects the academic staff to devote 25 percent of their research activities. Nevertheless, this did not happen due to overloading with teaching and administration, budget limitations, the inadequacy of infrastructure, and so forth.
Furthermore, apart from HERQA's study, various scholars researched the status of research practices at HEIs, secondary schools, and primary school levels. For example, [Derebssa (2000)](#page-6-0) studied the factors influencing research in the Institute of Education Research at Addis Ababa University and found that the university's marginalized research practice required further improvement. As reviewed above, various scholars and organizations, both global (United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization[ UNESCO, 1998](#page-7-0)) and local [(Derebssa, 2004;](#page-6-0) [FDRE, 2009](#page-6-0)), believe that higher education academic staff should recognize that research is one of their essential assignments in institutions.
The turning point in choosing the university was the absence or lack of similar studies investigating the practice of research in secondgeneration universities such as Madda Walabu University. Most studies were reviewed at first-generation universities, such as Bahir Dar, Mekele, Hawasa, and Addis Ababa Universities. On top of this, universities appear to be emphasizing research practices by establishing RCSD. Thus, the researcher was interested in exploring whether the established RCSD enhanced the research undertaken at the university. In line with this understanding, assessing faculty involvement in the target university has become necessary and timely.
### *1.2.* *Research questions *
The study aimed to answer the following research questions.
- (1) What factors influence research productions in the social, natural, and pedagogical science institutes? - (2) How are faculty members involved in research activities in the Social, Natural, and Pedagogical Science institutes?
#### *1.3.* *Significance of the study *
This study is crucial to shed light on the importance of scientific research in reducing poverty in Africa and Ethiopia in particular. It also initiates scholars to engage in scholarly investigations to facilitate individual and national economic development.
#### **2.** **Literature review **
### *2.1.* *Research productivity *
Research is an ongoing process in which we seek the truth or attempt to come close to reality. New problems are identified, data or information concerning those problems is collected, conclusions are drawn, and recommendations are made ([Gunawan, 2020](#page-6-0);[ Iqbal et al., 2018](#page-6-0);[ Iqbal ](#page-6-0)& [Mahmood, 2011)](#page-6-0). Researchers collect data, analyze data, explain data, and verify facts; research corrects errors; research advances knowledge. Research-based knowledge is always impartial and scientific. Knowledge derived through research is usually logical, rational, and based on experience. For[ Pinar and Unlu (2020),](#page-7-0) research is a deliberate endeavor to gather, verify, and analyze information.
The term "research productivity" combines two words: "research" and "productivity." "Research" refers to a thorough, observant inquiry into phenomena to discover new details, information, and facts ([Henry ](#page-6-0) [et al., 2020)](#page-6-0). In comparison, "productivity" refers to the amount of work or output generated during a period. Both of those terms have distinct connotations for various people. The publication of papers in professional journals, the publication of books, or the presentation of research papers in conference proceedings are examples of research production in higher education (Iqbal & [Mahmood, 2011)](#page-6-0).
### *2.2.* *Factors affecting research practices in higher education institutions *
Various factors influence academics' research engagement and output. Most scholars have conducted studies on this topic in developed countries. We can categorize the determining factors into individual, institutional, and national factors.
#### *2.2.1.* *Individual-level factors *
Numerous personal traits of academics have been discovered to significantly impact their research engagement and productivity [(Bland ](#page-6-0) [et al., 2005](#page-6-0); [Kwiek, 2016)](#page-7-0). Demographic, professional, psychological, and attitudinal traits all play a role. Furthermore, this review mainly considers significant aspects commonly mentioned in the literature.
Various factors are included in institutional-level factors. The age of the faculty influences research engagement and productivity ([Albert ](#page-6-0) [et al., 2016;](#page-6-0) [Kwiek, 2018](#page-7-0); [Vuong et al., 2017)](#page-7-0), academic rank ([Eam, ](#page-6-0) [2015;](#page-6-0)[ Nasser-Abu, Alhija ](#page-7-0)& Majdob, 2017), academic discipline [(Jung, ](#page-6-0) [2012;](#page-6-0) Shin & [Cummings, 2010)](#page-7-0), time spent on research ([Snowball ](#page-7-0)& [Shackleton, 2018)](#page-7-0), international collaboration ([Kwiek, 2018;](#page-7-0) [Nguyen ](#page-7-0) [et al., 2017](#page-7-0); [Ryan, 2014](#page-7-0); [Vuong et al., 2019)](#page-7-0), the language of research and publication ([Flowerdew, 2015](#page-6-0); Lillis & [Curry, 2010)](#page-7-0), intrinsic motivation ([Chen et al., 2006](#page-6-0); [Kwiek, 2016](#page-7-0)), desire for recognition (Snowball & [Shackleton, 2018)](#page-7-0), and research self-efficacy [(Eam, 2015](#page-6-0); Quimbo & [Sulabo, 2014](#page-7-0)).
#### *2.2.2.* *Institutional-level factors *
Organizational physical appearance has a remarkable effect on academics' research performance. The availability of resources and funding, institutional orientation, institutional research policies, institutional culture, reward and incentive systems, leadership styles,
and the availability of top researchers are all key institutional aspects that have been studied in past research [(Bland et al., 2005](#page-6-0); [Dundar ](#page-6-0)& [Lewis, 1998](#page-6-0); Quimbo & [Sulabo, 2014; Tien, 2016](#page-7-0)).
Institutional-level factors affect research engagement and productivity. Among others, institutions' research policy, teaching loads, availability of research funding, availability of professional meetings ([Nguyen, 2015)](#page-7-0), supportive attitude of administrative staff, institutional goal orientation and institutional mission [(Negash et al., 2019](#page-7-0); [Shin ](#page-7-0)& [Cummings, 2010)](#page-7-0), institutional support for research activity ([Borg ](#page-6-0)& [Alshumaimeri, 2012;](#page-6-0) [Ragasa, 2016](#page-7-0)), research benefits and incentives ([Phuong et al., 2017;](#page-7-0) Quimbo & [Sulabo, 2014](#page-7-0);[ Tien, 2016)](#page-7-0), and a culture that values research [(Bland et al., 2005;](#page-6-0) [Negash et al., 2019;](#page-7-0) [Pornsal](#page-7-0)[nuwat, 2014](#page-7-0)).
### *2.2.3.* *National-level factors *
At a national level, factors such as government rules, culture, academic freedom, government investment, industrial support, development partners, and international donor agencies significantly impact academics' and institutions' research performance. Although most studies on faculty research engagement and productivity focus on individual and institutional factors ([Bland et al., 2005](#page-6-0); [Chen et al., 2006](#page-6-0); [Pornsalnuwat, 2014;](#page-7-0) Quimbo & [Salabu, 2014](#page-7-0)), macro-level appearances can have significant impacts on scholars' and research productivity, particularly in the context of developing and emerging economies ([Negash et al., 2019;](#page-7-0) Quimbo & [Salabu, 2014;](#page-7-0) Sam & [Dahles, 2017](#page-7-0); [Tien, 2016)](#page-7-0).
National-level factors that affect research involvement include socioeconomic, sociocultural, and political factors ([Tien, 2016](#page-7-0)), politically sensitive issues [(Cambodian Institute for Cooperation and Peace (CICP), ](#page-6-0) [2016)](#page-6-0), respondents' unwillingness to provide a genuine response ([Morgenbesser ](#page-7-0)& Weiss, 2018), government and private sectors' research support [(Pornsalnuwat, 2014](#page-7-0)), and donor agencies [(Fussy, ](#page-6-0) [2017;](#page-6-0)[ Rappleye ](#page-7-0)& Un, 2018; [Salmi, 2017;](#page-7-0) Sam & [Dahles, 2017](#page-7-0)). Especially in developing countries, donors heavily control research funds. According to [UNESCO](#page-7-0)'s (2015) report, several African countries allocated less than 1% of their GDP to research and development, with bilateral and multilateral donors accounting for about 90% of research financing ([Kraemer-Mbula ](#page-6-0)& Scerri, 2015;[ Urama et al., 2015)](#page-7-0).
### **3.** **Materials and methods **
#### *3.1.* *Research design *
The study has employed a case study design. Other qualitative methodologies, such as ground theory or phenomenology, are usually not able to provide the same degree of freedom as case study research ([Meyer, 2001](#page-7-0)). According to [Bogdan and Biklen (2007),](#page-6-0) the case study approach enabled the researcher to investigate the academic staff's perception of research production through real-life experience at Madda Walabu University. Because of three strong arguments, the researcher decided to conduct a qualitative case study. First, by acquiring data from diverse colleges using the same approaches and techniques, the design aids in improving the transferability and reliability of outcomes in the three colleges [(Yin, 1981)](#page-7-0). Second, the design also enables one to highlight trends and disparities while providing a comprehensive account of each circumstance (Bogdan & [Biklen, 2007)](#page-6-0). Finally, the design supports the portrayal of research and theory development [(Creswell, ](#page-6-0) [2009)](#page-6-0). The current state of research production is evaluated to enhance the importance of research productivity in tertiary education ([Yin, ](#page-7-0) [2014)](#page-7-0). Since this study explored issues related to research production with the specific focus of Madda Walabu University, a case study design was appropriate.
### *3.2.* *Key informants *
The researcher recruited key informants for interviews and focus
group discussions (FGD). Accordingly, the study has selected the college deans and the school's research focal people (research coordinators) using a purposive sampling technique since the directors have the power to influence research practices positively or negatively. Again, research facilitators were critical as they coordinated research practices in each college. The three colleges had seven departments. To that end, the study selected one respondent from each department using a purposive sampling technique based on their research participation. The inclusion of each department was due to the enthusiasm for knowing the faculty's degree of research engagement in their respective schools.
The researcher contacted and discussed with three of the college's research coordinators, who know the issues under study and the university's overall context better than the other faculty, to obtain suitable informants. The study has selected key informants with rich information based on the discussion with research focal persons based on the following criteria: years of teaching experience in the institutes, level of qualification, involvement in the research, and willingness to participate. Considering these factors, the researcher has recruited 13 informants (six for interviews—three school directors and three school's research focal persons, and seven for FGD) for the study.
#### *3.3.* *Instruments of data collection *
Interviews, FGD, and document analysis were data collection instruments. From Merriam'[s (1998) ](#page-7-0)perspective, the qualitative case study's data collection approaches are exciting interviews, careful observation, and document analyses. Besides, [Wellington (1996) ](#page-7-0) mentioned that FGD is also a complementary technique for collecting qualitative case studies.
#### *3.3.1.* *Interview *
The researcher employed interviews to gain detailed information from the informants about the university's research production status. The researcher interviewed six informants since their numbers were not too large; this tool allowed for clarifications and greater flexibility. It enabled the researcher to observe non-verbal communication [(Newman, ](#page-7-0) [2007)](#page-7-0). The audio equipment supported the interviewing process after the researcher asked permission to use a tape recorder. Tape recording helped minimize the loss of information during the interview process. For the following reasons, they allowed me to use a voice recorder: First, the principal researcher, the college deans, and the research coordinators know each other and have a good rapport as we work in the same institution. Second, the Academic Vice President of the University wrote letters of cooperation to the colleges, and the college deans told the selected faculty to cooperate with me.
Besides, the researcher took detailed notes during the interview just in case of incompatibility with a tape recorder. By initiating the interviewees, the researcher forwarded questions related to personal inputs (such as their skills, competencies, interests, commitments, and specializations), financial and material inputs, and incentives to the respondents. Thus, on average, the interview process took 30–40 minutes min from May 29–June 7, 2018. Concerning the place of the interview, the researcher interviewed informants in their offices. For clarity, the researcher conducted all interviews in Amharic (an official language of Ethiopia).
#### *3.3.2.* *Focus group discussion *
The study held focus group discussions (FGD) with seven university faculties from seven departments because their interactions provided a thorough grasp of the extent of research productivity in three colleges. The reason to use FGD was to get more robust and versatile information. Besides, FGD helped me understand issues with consensus and variations among departments and has shown a different orientation towards research. FGDs are inexpensive and data-rich, engaging participants and supporting them in important occurrences, allowing them to advance beyond the responses of only one individual interviewed [(Newman, ](#page-7-0)
[2007)](#page-7-0). FGD has drawbacks when one person serves as both the interviewer and the note-taker during interviews ([Flick, 2009)](#page-6-0); to get around this problem, the researcher hired one expert to record the group interview responses without taking on additional duties for the whole FGD. The researcher oversaw the group interview and served as a discussion facilitator. He also developed structured discussion guidelines. One group interview is held during the FGD. The content of the discussion revolved around factors hindering research productivity in their colleges. We have utilized the Amharic language for FGD because we believe that informants and researcher communicate better in Amharic than in English. The conference typically lasted for 2 hours and ran on April 6, 2018.
### *3.3.3.* *Document analysis *
In qualitative studies, document analysis is one of the primary data collection tools [(Merriam, 1998)](#page-7-0). The study investigated and analyzed the three institutes' timetables to collect information about the faculty's teaching load. Besides, the researcher has analyzed Madda Walabu research policy documents. Madda Walabu University's research policy involves three documents. These are guidelines for proposal writing, the university's intellectual property policy, community engagement, and research policies.
### *3.4.* *Methods of data analysis *
[Bogdan and Biklen (2007)](#page-6-0) suggested two data analysis and interpretation approaches. In the first approach, the researcher conduct data analysis and interpretation concurrently. The authors usually recommend this method to experienced researchers. The authors recommend another approach for the beginner, which analyses and interprets data after collecting it. As a novice researcher, he preferred the latter approach for analyzing and interpreting data.
The study employed the NVivo 11 qualitative analysis software program for data analysis. Concerning the analysis approach, the study used the six-stage thematic analysis approach suggested by [Braun and ](#page-6-0) [Clarke (2006)](#page-6-0). The researcher invited two linguists to translate the Amharic version of the transcription into English, and they handed over 200 pages of English transcriptions. The second stage involved uploading the interview transcripts onto the NVivo 11 program. The investigator discovered 300 codes. In step three, the researcher identified 10 themes pertaining to hindering factors for research productivity after listening to the voice recordings and reading the transcription repeatedly. Fourth, as a result of the researcher's identification of themes and sub-themes, many themes, including related concepts, emerged. In stage five, each theme's nature was differentiated, its essential problems were identified, and the categories of data that each theme understood were specified. Various themes are investigated in this stage, which[ Braun and ](#page-6-0) [Clarke (2006) ](#page-6-0)refer to as a "subsequent refining stage," to ascertain the stories that each informs. When the theme was being refined, it looked at how each theme aligned with the general objectives of the study and how the data supported the research questions. To lessen excessive theme crossover, the refining method was developed. Consequently, two main themes were identified: factors related to personal input and institutional facilities. The researcher supported the themes in the reports in stage six by using direct quotations.
### *3.5.* *Ethical consideration *
The researcher protected the participants' security in the following ways: before the commencement of fieldwork, he described the study's purpose and requested the Academic Vice President of the University for the Formal Permission to access the study site, and consent was secured from participants. The researcher kept their identities anonymous.
### **4.** **Results and discussions **
The collected data revealed two broad categories of factors that negatively contribute to faculty involvement in research activities. These categories are personal and institutional factors (inputs). Before presenting these factors in detail, knowing the background information of informants seems essential.
#### *4.1.* *The background of key informants *
The study recruited 11 male and two female faculty members based on specified criteria. Their field of specialization varies. For instance, the study recruited vocational management, history, geography, educational leadership, biology, chemistry, sport science, and curriculum and instruction faculty for interviews and FGD. The participants also held different faculty positions, such as faculty directors, heads of departments, and coordinators of different programs. Faculty had served 3–7 years at Madda Walabu University. However, most respondents had been teaching at secondary schools and colleges before joining the university.
#### *4.2.* *Data analysis of factors affecting research practices *
The investigation revealed two broad themes that hindered research practices: individual-related factors and institutional-related factors. Individual-related factors involve four sub-themes: faculty's skills and competence, faculty's perception of research, faculty members' interest in conducting research, and faculty specializations. The themes and their sub-themes are presented in detail.
### *4.2.1.* *Individual-related factors *
*4.2.1.1.* *Faculty members**' **skills and competencies.* Equipping research knowledge and skills is vital to engaging in practical research activities. Supporting this,[ Weiler et al. (2008) ](#page-7-0)state that research capacity consists primarily, though by no means exclusively, of people capable of conducting research—faculty, research staff, and graduate students. In line with this issue, the study presented the following discussions.
Most informants who participated in the study agreed on research capacity. They stressed that faculty from educational backgrounds such as curriculum and instruction, educational planning and management, educational leadership, and educational psychology have a better research orientation. Conversely, faculty from natural science backgrounds capitalized on the fact that anyone with an MA or MSC degree in any field of study can engage in research practices through independent reading. According to them, a lack of prior research knowledge is not a hindering factor for faculty engagement in the research.
The other informants remarked that the lack of research in their department is a prominent obstacle to research production. Further, they stated that the problem is not of equal magnitude for all faculties; instead, it is severe for natural science faculty because their training gives minimal orientation about research methodology. One of the interviewees firmly remarked in this manner:
As a mathematics faculty member, I need training on how to apply different statistical tools in research production. We did a project during our MSc but did not get involved in doing a thesis; thus, we did not engage in any research activity in a broader way (I6).
Others, however, contradicted the above expression. For instance, I3 said:
We have taken courses in research methods, statistics, sampling, data collection, and data analysis techniques at the graduate and undergraduate levels. However, the research culture, the lack of a research budget, and the absence of incentives hindered research production.
In the FGD, participants have had a heated discussion concerning the faculty's research knowledge. Concerning the issue, the group was divided into two; one said that someone with a second degree in any field of study could enhance their research capacity through additional reading. Conversely, the second group argued that research knowledge is fundamental to engaging in it initially. Lastly, all the members of FGD, except F2 from the first group, agreed that research knowledge is essential. The FGD discussion about evaluating the role of their skills in conducting research revealed that almost all participants came to terms with their prior skills' inadequacy. From the discussion, this study revealed that the acquisition of necessary skills in research is vital. According to most informants, prior skills' inadequacy is one problem that impedes faculty involvement in research. This finding resonates with [Iqbal and Mahmood](#page-6-0)'s (2011) findings. They found that some faculties lack the research skills to conduct research.
*4.2.1.2.* *Faculty perceptions toward research.* Perception is how an individual perceives any event in the world and the world itself [(Morgan ](#page-7-0) [et al., 1986](#page-7-0)). The faculty's perception of educational research and their ultimate involvement in educational research may result from acquiring knowledge and skills in educational research methods and educational practices and the subsequent appreciation of its attributes. This subsection presents the faculty's perception of educational research.
Most informants did not perceive research engagement as part of their regular duties. I3, for instance, explained how he understands research in this way: "For me, research is not a mandatory role for faculty. If it were our primary duty, just like teaching, there would have been some penalty in the case of failure to conduct research." Furthermore, participants, including directors (the dean), believe that the university hired them mainly for teaching purposes.
However, some faculties believe that conducting research is their obligation. I1 argues in this fashion: "As a university faculty member, I must engage in research to combat societal problems. Even to deliver participatory teaching-learning processes, involvement in research is paramount." On his part, another participant (I5) perceived research as an expensive, complex, and difficult task to accomplish at this level without solid institutional backing. Nevertheless, there are research activities that require few resources, such as action research.
In the FGD, most informants do not see research practice as their regular duty. Faculty misconceptions contributed to their low involvement in research activity. From the discussion above, one can infer that when the university appoints faculty, they have no awareness of research. Most faculties replied that research is not their responsibility, which implies that the university lacks a research culture. This finding agrees with the findings of[ Derebssa (2004)](#page-6-0). They found out that their respective research settings lacked research cultures.
*4.2.1.3.* *Lack of research interest.* Interest is a major driving force behind any activity because interest in any activity is self-derived. Therefore, the faculty's interest in research affects their involvement in research activities. Most informants believe that most faculty members are less interested in research activities. According to I3, "if they had a genuine interest in conducting research, they would have participated in a type of research (e.g., action research) that needs fewer resources." However, a few participants claim that faculty members have an interest in engaging in research production. I6 argues the existence of an interest in this way:
Some faculty members are interested in research activities for two compelling reasons: First, to achieve academic status and promotion, faculty must conduct research and publish in peer-reviewed journals. Secondly, research involvement enhances faculty income sources.
Similarly, most FGD participants have expressed faculty members' lack of research interest. Generally, from the discussion of interviews and FGDs, most faculty in the schools lack interest in conducting
research. This finding goes with[ Iqbal and Mahmood](#page-6-0)'s (2011) finding. They found that the faculty had a negative attitude towards research.
### *4.2.2.* *Institutional-related factors *
No matter how skilled an individual is and how interested they are in engaging in research productions, facility availability determines their success [(Lehtien, 1990)](#page-7-0). This theme involves a lack of material or facility, a lack of incentives, the nature of the staff, time availability, a lengthy research administration procedure, and thematic research areas.
*4.2.2.1.* *Lack of material/facilities to conduct research.* For research activities to flourish, it is necessary to have a conducive research environment with infrastructure and equipment. Some necessary physical facilities are databases, libraries, documentation centers, and good communication [(Derebssa, 2000](#page-6-0)). Institutional support and stationery materials are necessary to encourage potential researchers to engage in research.
Most informants expressed the existence of poor facilities such as the library, office equipment, and other services. For example, one of the school directors said, "Currently, the internet is the source of knowledge that provides up-to-date information concerning the problem under study. However, it is difficult to find relevant information because of the poor internet connection " (I1). Apart from this, there was also a lack of articles and journals. For instance, I3 states the issue in this manner: "In our university, it is difficult to find the latest articles since there is a shortage of journals that provide information to the researchers." The remaining interviewees focus on the shortage of offices and computers. For instance, I5 argues as follows:
Our university lacks offices. In our department, 15 faculty members use one small room as a staff office, and this office has only five chairs and three tables. Because of this, the office serves five faculties at a time.
Still, others underline the shortage of computers. For five faculties, there is only one desktop computer. At the time of data collection, the provision of laptops was only for administrative personnel*. *
In the FGD, all the participants agreed on a lack of internet services, articles, offices, and computers. From the above discussion, a lack of relevant literature and educational documents, a lack of internet access, and office facilities characterize the status of the faculty's involvement in research. Therefore, insufficient material inputs hinder the faculty's involvement in research activities. This finding is consistent with Wudu'[s (2013)](#page-7-0) and[ Cocal et al.](#page-6-0)'s (2017) findings. They found that their respective universities lacked the materials and facilities to partake in research.
*4.2.2.2.* *Lack of incentives.* The range of incentives is crucial for taking part in the research. It includes the availability of funds for research work, academic promotion based on research involvement, reducing teaching load, an inducement for writing articles, and long-term subsidies to the journal. Concerning incentives, almost all the informants in the interviews stressed the institution's weaknesses in encouraging research work. For instance, one interviewee states it this way:
Faculty does not receive incentives of any kind for their research undertakings. Additionaly, the university does not provide any incentive to conduct research or publish findings in peer-reviewed journals. Nonetheless, a research grant is an initial condition for engaging in research (I2).
However, some interviewees argued that, though research funding is crucial, it is possible to conduct action research that tackles immediate solutions to teaching and learning processes. For instance, I6 argues in this fashion: "I do not know why people mention a lack of research funds as a serious hindering factor to engaging in research production. For instance, the faculty can participate in action research that does not
require much money."
The FGD's stress on the lack of incentives or a research budget hindered research undertakings at the university. In general, they argue that the incentive to conduct research is insignificant. When faculties try to participate in research, the university does not provide copy and print services.
The university's research policy document analysis shows no incentive issues that encourage investigators except the following: "A researcher who secures funding from external sources is subjected to a financial reward based on the agreement made with the funding organization. However, it should not exceed ten percent of the budget granted." From the above discussion, the incentives for researchers are meager at the institution. Therefore, very poor incentives do not encourage faculty involvement in research practices. This finding resonates with the findings of [Abate and Selamawit (2015),](#page-6-0) [Nguyen and ](#page-7-0) [Klopper (2014)](#page-7-0), and[ Sanyal and Varghese (2006)](#page-7-0). They found that their respective research settings lack incentives that encourage teachers to participate in research.
*4.2.2.3.* *Lack of staff**'**s research skills.* The nature of the staff who work together can influence the faculty's involvement in all research activities. In connection with this issue, the discussions by the study's informants are as follows. Most of the informants who participated in the interview and FGD agreed that their faculties' main problems are the absence of well-skilled and experienced faculty in the research practices. For instance, one interviewee states, "Due to the university's being in a remote area, it has been recruiting fresh graduates for teaching-learning processes. Because of this, most of the faculties have no research experience " (I6). Similarly, another interviewee argues that "our university lacks experienced researchers because the experienced researchers neither want to join the university nor stay at the university to obtain better job opportunities" (I3).
Conversely, there was a counterargument to the above. Others state that there were some experienced researchers, but they did not want to cooperate with fresh faculty members. I2, for example, argues that "experienced researchers were involuntarily working with fresh graduates because they undermined new faculty. Besides, the collaborative culture at the university is shallow."
Similarly, the discussions also show that a severe shortage of research skills prevails in each faculty because they recruit fresh graduates and leave experienced faculty at the university. In summary, a lack of research skills and collaboration among experienced and novice faculty hindered research practices. This finding goes with the findings of [Henry et al. (2020)](#page-6-0). They found that faculties lack the skills to participate in research work
*4.2.2.4.* *Lack of time to conduct research.* It takes significant time to conduct research and publish the findings in peer-reviewed journals ([Cocal et al., 2017](#page-6-0)). According to university policy, academic staff should devote 25% of their time to engaging in research. The following paragraphs examine faculty members' workloads. All the informants expressed that a shortage of time was not their primary problem in participating in the research activity. I1 argues the issue of time in this manner:
In our school, there is no work pressure. We have ample time to engage in research since we have three to six credit hours per week. Moreover, we have no extension classes or distance courses. Thus, faculties have ample time to involve themselves in research.
Similarly, (I3) affirmed the availability of time for faculty to participate in research work. He said that he had only taken two courses in a year. Therefore, for him, the workload does not affect faculty members' involvement in research.
Also, in the FGD, all the discussants agreed that workload is not the determining factor. While university legislation allows 12 credit hours,
faculty members have six or fewer credit hours per week. Thus, the faculty's workload is not a significant problem that hinders faculty members involvement in research. The review of the timetables in the three schools also supports the nonexistence of time pressure. While analyzing the timetables, the average credit hour for social science, natural science, and pedagogical science institutes is six credit hours per week.
From the above discussion, one can infer that the faculty's workload is not the main impediment to faculty members' involvement in research. Thus, faculty have ample time to participate in research if conditions and facilities such as a research budget, books and journals, and internet services are available, along with personal interest. This finding is different from previous findings. Differently, [Nguyen et al. ](#page-7-0) [(2021) ](#page-7-0)found that the faculty had a heavy workload that did not leave space for research activities.
*4.2.2.5.* *Prolonged research administration procedure.* Since the establishment of RCSD, it has administered all research practices. The views of different informants about the procedures of research administration at the university are as follows. All the informants said tedious research administration procedures affect research practice. Concerning this idea, one of the directors said we cannot manage research activities since the RCSD centrally administers the research budget. Supporting this, one of the schools' research focal persons explained:
Here at Madda Walabu University, a research proposal should pass through different stages. First, a researcher defends a proposal at the departmental level, and to continue to the next level, one needs to have 55 percent or above. Second, after scoring 55 and above, a researcher defends the proposal at the school level, and to continue in the system, a researcher needs a score of sixty percent and above. Finally, a researcher presents and defends the university-level proposal to obtain budget approval (I4).
Most of the interview participants agreed with such tedious research administration procedures. However, some interview participants see this prolonged administration as a good thing. According to these informants, it becomes verified when research passes through different levels and yields promising findings. For instance, I5 states as follows:
When a researcher defends a proposal at the department level, the evaluators will add some valuable comments to the proposal. If they present it at the school level, it would be better at this stage to incorporate school-level evaluators' comments and feedback to participate in the final defense at the university level.
However, most faculty members doubt the evaluators' research expertise to provide genuine comments on the proposed research. Since the university has fresh graduates for faculty positions, it is challenging to find experienced researchers at each department and school level.
In supporting the lengthy research administration procedure, the discussants in the FGD mentioned the following reasons: Even proposals that pass the initial two stages have a high chance of failing at the university level because the university-level evaluators do not have the skill to evaluate research proposals. The above data shows that the strong centralization of research administration and the various presentation levels affected research practices. This finding goes with[ Henry ](#page-6-0) et al.'[s (2020)](#page-6-0) finding. They found that the research policy of their study area affected research production.
## **5.** **Conclusions **
Instructors are liable to be involved in research activities to ensure the quality of education in HEIs. Besides, as mentioned in the Ministry of Education Proclamation and the university legislation, the university expects the higher education academic staff to conduct research. However, the study found that most instructors in the three colleges are not
engaged in research activities for various reasons. For instance, a lack of research skills, lengthy research administration procedures, a lack of facilities, a shortage of funds to conduct research, and a weak research culture are severe challenges to research practices at the university. The study revealed that institutional factors and faculty input affected faculty involvement in research activities. Therefore, the status of the research undertaking is in the infancy stage.
This study has various strengths. One of the serious issues to be answered in qualitative research is a methodological rigor. The following procedures were used to guarantee methodological rigor: First, information was obtained from several groups of people, including college deans, research facilitators, and academic staff. Second, information was acquired through various research techniques (interviews, focus group discussions, and document analysis). The researcher then gave the transcriptions to college deans and research facilitators to determine if the transcriptions matched their responses after transcribing the data. Therefore, it was the researcher's responsibility to accurately and in-depth characterize each participant's point of view.
Finally, this study also has a limitation. While there are 8 colleges in the university, the researcher used only 3 and involved 13 participants. Hence, it is difficult to generalize for all colleges found in the university. Hence, future quantitative studies are important to enhance the external validity of research.
### **6.** **Recommendations **
Infrastructural challenges take the lead in affecting the teaching staff's research activity in the faculties. The university needs to consider significant issues such as a lack of internet services, a lack of up-to-date reference materials, uncomfortable offices, and a lack of laptops. Besides, the university should tackle problems such as a budget shortage for research and the absence of researchers' incentives through different mechanisms.
The research administration process seems strongly centralized because all research proposals need to be presented and defended at the university level after passing the initial two stages and having a high chance of failure. Therefore, the university should allocate budgets, authority, and responsibility to the individual schools, as they have the right experts and responsible bodies to improve educational problems through research in their fields.

Dr. Aklilu Alemu is an assistant professor of Education Policy and Leadership at Madawalabu University in the Department of Educational Planning and Management of Ethiopia. He attained all his diplomas and degrees in Educational Planning, Leadership, Policy, and Management at Addis Ababa University, and his prior experiences include teaching and managing primary schools and leading the educational program teams at the District Education Office. At Madawalabu University, he has taught and supervised undergraduate and graduate students, conducted research, and presented the findings at fifteen national and international conferences. Besides, he has published three articles and one book.
